query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor alloying addition of boron (around 0.1 at.%) to equiatomic BCC NbMoTaW followed by a controlled thermal treatment will promote the formation of fine, intergranular boride precipitates that enhance grain-boundary cohesion. This, in turn, will improve the alloy’s room-temperature ductility and mitigate irradiation-induced damage (e.g., helium blistering) while preserving its high-temperature strength and phase stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW that exhibits excellent high‐temperature strength (up to ~1600 °C) but poor ductility at room temperature; its irradiation resistance has been mostly inferred from computational studies.
generation.intervention: Introduce approximately 0.1 at.% boron into the NbMoTaW matrix and apply a controlled annealing (thermal processing) schedule designed to produce a uniform dispersion of fine boride precipitates along the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Mechanical (tensile and nanoindentation) testing at room temperature to evaluate ductility; high-temperature tests up to 1600 °C to ensure phase stability and strength retention; and dual-beam irradiation (e.g., heavy ions plus He implantation) performed at reactor-relevant temperatures (around 1073–1173 K) and fluences to simulate both helium and displacement damage.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanometer-scale boride precipitates distributed at grain boundaries that increase grain-boundary cohesion and act as effective sinks or barriers to irradiation-induced defects.
generation.mechanism: The minor boron addition is expected to trigger the precipitation of fine boride phases at the grain boundaries. These precipitates strengthen the interface, thereby reducing intergranular fracture (improving ductility) and lowering the nucleation sites for irradiation-induced helium bubbles or precipitates. Concurrently, because the boride phase is finely dispersed and limited in volume fraction, the overall BCC matrix remains largely unaltered, preserving its high-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to unmodified NbMoTaW, the boron-modified alloy will exhibit significantly enhanced room-temperature ductility (higher elongation and improved work hardenability) and reduced signs of irradiation-induced blistering or amorphization, while retaining similar high-temperature strength and BCC phase stability.
generation.baseline: Unalloyed, equiatomic NbMoTaW, which shows excellent high-temperature properties but poor room-temperature ductility and whose irradiation response is only computationally predicted.
generation.boundary: The improvements are expected under conditions relevant to reactor service—room temperature for ductility and up to ~1600 °C for strength, with irradiation tests conducted at elevated temperatures (~1073–1173 K) and within fluence ranges typical for dual-beam experiments. Effects outside these ranges remain to be evaluated.
generation.uncertainty: While minor boron additions have been effective in other refractory HEA systems (e.g., HfMoNbTaTiZr as discussed in PMC9572892::web::015::4_conclusions) and microstructural inversion approaches have improved ductility (PMC5995863::web::021::discussion), it remains uncertain whether NbMoTaW will react similarly given its strongly bonded, single-phase BCC matrix. The risk is that excessive or uncontrolled boride precipitation might degrade high-temperature properties or introduce unwanted heterogeneity.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of NbMoTaW alloys: one as the control (pure equiatomic NbMoTaW) and the other with a minor (~0.1 at.%) boron addition. Both batches should undergo identical thermal processing designed to induce any potential boride precipitation. Perform room-temperature mechanical tests (tensile and nanoindentation), high-temperature tensile and creep tests up to 1600 °C, and dual-beam irradiation experiments (combining heavy ions and helium implantation) at elevated temperatures (around 1073–1173 K). Use microstructural characterization techniques (TEM, APT, XRD) to examine the presence, size, and distribution of boride precipitates and to assess irradiation-induced defect evolution.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile ductility (elongation, yield strength, and fracture mode)
High-temperature mechanical strength and phase stability (via XRD and TEM)
Irradiation-induced defect features (e.g., helium bubble size/density, blistering) via TEM and APT
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-modified NbMoTaW does not exhibit a statistically significant (e.g., >10%) improvement in room-temperature ductility and a reduction in irradiation-induced defects (such as blistering or amorphization) compared to the control, or if its high-temperature performance (strength and phase stability) degrades by more than 10%, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The thermal stability in terms of grain size is studied via in situ TEM annealing and irradiation and the results are plotted in Fig. 3. The average grain size of the as-deposited sample was 24.5 ± 1.3 nm. After annealing to 1173 K for ~30 mins in the TEM, the grain size increased to 26.3 ± 1.1 nm. After He implantation, the grain size further increased to 36.3 ± 1.8 nm. However, during the dual-beam irradiation, grain refinement occurred, and the average grain size dropped to 21.1 ± 1.4 nm after a total irradiation time of ~94 mins. The overall material stability in terms of phases and segregation is discussed further below. The irradiation resistance of the alloy is also studied in terms of both dislocation loop formation and cavity formation. Dislocation loops were not detected even after 8.5 dpa and at 9.13% He implantation during the dual-beam experiment (Supplementary Movie 1 is attached to the supplementary material). Only cavities were observed. Quantification of the cavity density, average cavity size, and total change in sample volume is shown in Fig. 4. In summary, careful microstructural examination of Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr was carried out in the present study using advanced TEM and APT techniques. The results reveal that the homogenized and slow cooled (~10 °C/min) microstructure (Condition (1)) has an ordered B2 phase as the continuous matrix, interspersed with discrete cuboidal-like pockets of a disordered BCC phase. While this microstructure morphologically resembles the γ (fcc) + γ’ (ordered L12) type microstructure observed in many Ni-base superalloys, it is “inverted” in the sense that the continuous matrix phase is the ordered B2 phase, resulting in limited compressive ductility. The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion. Consequently, the hard, ordered B2 compound that forms the continuous phase in Condition (1) is replaced by the more ductile, disordered, BCC phase in Condition (3). The resultant microstructurally-engineered RHEA not only exhibits high yield strength at room temperature (~1345 MPa) and 600 °C (~1423 MPa), but also substantial compressive ductility at room temperature (>20%). An equimolar HfMoNbTaTiZr RHEA was developed in this study, and the addition of a minor amount of boron (0.1 at.%, RHEA-B) further overcame the grain-boundary brittleness. As indicated by the microstructural observations and chemical analyses, a simple BCC-phase, solid-solution structure was formed in the matrices of both the alloys. The addition of boron did not obviously increase the hardness of the matrix but induced the intergranular precipitation of the HCP-phase (Hf, Zr)B2 borides which markedly raised the hardness of the grain boundaries. Attributable to the lattice distortions caused by the random distribution of different constituent elements, a diminished anisotropy in the mechanical properties was noticed, and the deformation behavior was mediated by many small slips on multiple {110} planes. Owing to the enhanced grain boundary cohesion with the addition of boron and the intergranular precipitation of borides, the work hardenability and ductility of the alloy were effectively improved, and the failure mode obviously changed from a mainly intergranular facture to a major portion of the transgranular fracture.
